newsitem.title: CHINA: China offers carrot backed by stick to rival Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China offers carrot backed by stick to rival Taiwan.

text.p: China said on Sunday it would send its most senior capitalist to Taiwan to ease strained ties but coupled the olive branch with an attack on attempts by its island arch-rival to rejoin the United Nations.

"Taiwan's attempt to 'rejoin the United Nations' will bring tensions between the two sides across the Taiwan Straits, and is doomed to failure," the official Xinhua news agency said in a commentary issued on Sunday.

Beijing has been enraged by a campaign by Taiwan, which China regards as a rebel province, to boost its international profile since the island's President Lee Teng-hui made a landmark private visit to the United States last year.

Xinhua accused the island's leaders of trying to deceive world opinion and their own people by professing commitment to eventual reunification with the mainland while quietly seeking support to raise Taiwan's international standing.

"The Taiwan authorities made use of 'the people's will', and cheated world opinion by creating a false appearance that the 'will of the people in Taiwan in favour of rejoining the U.N. is upsurging'," the commentary said.
It blasted attempts by Taiwan to build support for a bid to rejoin the United Nations, saying Taipei had instigated a group of Central American countries in July to support its re-entry.
Taiwan, which lost China's U.N. seat to Beijing in 1971, hopes that all 30 countries that recognise it instead of Beijing will help its bid to return to the world body.
"The farce directed by the Taiwan authorities to split the motherland cannot win people's will, so it will not help save their failure to 'rejoin the U.N.'," the commentary said.

Taipei had been trying to win support by selling itself as a "democracy", Xinhua scoffed, apparently referring to Taiwan's first direct presidential elections last March that returned President Lee to office with a resounding majority.

Communist Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since the Nationalist army fled to the island after losing the Chinese civil war in 1949, and Beijing says it must be brought under its rule -- by force if necessary.

However, Beijing extended a carrot as well as a stick to Taiwan, announcing that its most senior private-sector leader and capitalist was to lead a group of private businessmen to Taiwan in December on a visit aimed at improving relations.

Jing Shuping, chairman of the private-sector All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, would attend a meeting of entrepreneurs from China, Taiwan and Hong Kong in Taipei, the China Daily Business Weekly said.

The delegation would discuss Taiwanese investment in the mainland's agriculture, technology and other sectors and would try to direct more funds to China's lagging central and western regions, the newspaper said.
"It is very natural that we will touch on the far-reaching issue of establishing direct trade, postal and shipping services across the (Taiwan) Strait," it quoted Jing as saying.
China last month unilaterally issued regulations governing potential direct shipping and postal links with Taiwan, which sees such ties as its last bargaining chip with Beijing.
"Taiwan gains nothing from staying away from the mainland's natural resouces, labour and land," Jing said.
Taiwan's President Lee on Saturday accused China of using commerce as a political weapon and urged local companies to exercise restraint over their mainland investments.
Just weeks earlier he warned that the island was becoming too dependent on trade with the mainland.
Taiwanese investment in the mainland totalled more than $20 billion at the end of 1995.
